sections.title: Verbs Never Conjugate
sections.rule: Mandarin verbs have exactly one form regardless of subject or time. Tense is expressed by time words (昨天 yesterday, 明天 tomorrow) and aspect markers, not by changing the verb. The verb itself never adds endings.
sections.example_target: 我昨天去北京，明天去上海。
sections.example_ref: English: I went to Beijing yesterday, I go to Shanghai tomorrow. / He is very busy today.
sections.note: pinyin: wǒ zuótiān qù Běijīng, míngtiān qù Shànghǎi. Don't look for a 'past tense' of 去 — the time word does the work.

sections.title: Measure Words (量词)
sections.rule: Every counted noun needs a measure word (classifier) between the number and the noun: Number + Measure Word + Noun. Different nouns take different classifiers, but 个 (gè) is the safe default. 一本书, 三个人, 两条鱼.
sections.example_target: 我要三个苹果和一本书。
sections.example_ref: English: I want three apples and one book. / There are two fish on the table.
sections.note: pinyin: wǒ yào sān gè píngguǒ hé yì běn shū. Flat things use 张, books use 本, long thin things use 条.

sections.title: Aspect Marker 了 (le)
sections.rule: 了 marks a completed action or a change of state, not past tense. 我吃了 = I ate / I have eaten; 我吃 = I eat. It can also signal 'now the situation is different'.
sections.example_ref: English: I have eaten. / It's raining now (it started to rain).
sections.note: pinyin: wǒ chī le fàn. / xià yǔ le. 了 is about completion or change, so 我每天吃了 is wrong — habitual actions take no 了.

sections.title: Markers 过 and 着
sections.rule: 过 (guo) marks a past experience ('have ever done'): 我去过北京. 着 (zhe) marks an ongoing or durative state: 他站着 (he is standing), 门开着 (the door is open).
sections.example_ref: English: I have been to Beijing (before). / The door is open.
sections.note: pinyin: wǒ qù guo Běijīng. / mén kāi zhe. 过 = experience at some point; 着 = a state that continues.

sections.title: Word Order: Time and Place
sections.rule: The core order is Subject + Time + Place + Verb + Object. Time and place come BEFORE the verb, unlike English. 我今天在家吃饭.
sections.example_ref: English: I eat at home today. / He has a meeting at the company tomorrow.
sections.note: pinyin: wǒ jīntiān zài jiā chīfàn. Never put place after the verb: 我吃饭在家 is wrong.

sections.title: The 把 Construction
sections.rule: 把 (bǎ) moves the object in front of the verb to stress what is done to it: Subject + 把 + Object + Verb + Result/Location. Used when the object is specific and something happens to it. 把书放在桌子上.
sections.example_ref: English: Please close the door. / I finished writing the homework.
sections.note: pinyin: qǐng bǎ mén guān shàng. The verb in a 把 sentence usually needs a result (完, 上, 好), not a bare verb.

sections.title: Comparison with 比
sections.rule: Compare with A + 比 + B + Adjective: 他比我高 (He is taller than me). For the negative, use A + 没有 + B + Adjective: 我没有他高 (I'm not as tall as him).
sections.example_ref: English: He is taller than me. / Today is not as cold as yesterday.
sections.note: pinyin: tā bǐ wǒ gāo. Never add 很 with 比: 他比我很高 is wrong — say 他比我高一点/高得多.

sections.title: Asking Questions
sections.rule: For yes/no questions, add 吗 to a statement: 你去吗? For content questions, put the question word (什么 what, 哪里 where, 谁 who, 怎么 how, 为什么 why, 几 how many) in the SAME slot as the answer — word order does not change.
sections.example_ref: English: Where are you going? / What is this?
sections.note: pinyin: nǐ qù nǎlǐ? / zhè shì shénme? Chinese does not move the question word to the front like English does.

sections.title: Possession and 的 (de)
sections.rule: 的 links a modifier to a noun: Noun/Adj + 的 + Noun. 我的书 (my book), 老师的车 (the teacher's car), 红色的花 (red flower). It marks possession and description alike.
sections.example_ref: English: This is my book. / I like red flowers.
sections.note: pinyin: zhè shì wǒ de shū. Drop 的 for close relationships and body: 我妈妈, 我们学校 sound more natural than 我的妈妈.

sections.title: 两 vs 二 (liǎng vs èr)
sections.rule: Use 两 (liǎng) before a measure word to mean 'two of something': 两个, 两本. Use 二 (èr) for counting and within numbers: 十二 (twelve), 第二 (second), 二月 (February).
sections.example_ref: English: I have two children. / It is now February 12th.
sections.note: pinyin: wǒ yǒu liǎng gè háizi. Rule of thumb: '2 + measure word' → 两; '2 inside a number' → 二.

sections.title: Resultative Complements
sections.rule: Attach a second verb/adjective to show the result of an action: Verb + Result. 看见 (see/perceive), 听懂 (understand by listening), 吃完 (finish eating), 找到 (find, succeed in locating).
sections.example_ref: English: I understood what the teacher said. / I found my phone.
sections.note: pinyin: wǒ tīngdǒng le lǎoshī de huà. The first verb is the action, the second is whether it succeeded — 看 (look) vs 看见 (actually see).

sections.title: Directional Complements
sections.rule: Add 来 (toward speaker) or 去 (away from speaker) after a motion verb to show direction: 进来 (come in), 出去 (go out), 回来 (come back), 上去 (go up).
sections.example_ref: English: Please come in. / Has he come back?
sections.note: pinyin: qǐng jìn lái. Choose 来/去 from the speaker's position: standing outside you say 进去 (go in), standing inside you say 进来 (come in).

sections.title: The 是...的 Construction
sections.rule: 是...的 highlights the time, place, or manner of an action already known to have happened: 我是昨天来的. The 是 goes before the highlighted detail and 的 comes at the end.
sections.example_ref: English: I came by plane (it was by plane that I came). / He was born in Beijing.
sections.note: pinyin: wǒ shì zuò fēijī lái de. Use it to stress HOW/WHEN/WHERE a known past event happened, not to report new events.

sections.title: Potential Complements 得/不
sections.rule: Insert 得 (can) or 不 (cannot) between a verb and its result to show ability/possibility: 听得懂 (can understand) vs 听不懂 (can't understand); 吃得完 vs 吃不完 (can/can't finish).
sections.example_target_2: 你说慢一点我就听得懂。
sections.example_ref: English: So much food — I can't finish it. / If you speak slower I can understand.
sections.note: pinyin: zhème duō cài, wǒ chī bu wán. Different from 不能吃完: the 得/不 form is about inherent possibility, not permission.

sections.title: 会 / 能 / 可以 Modals
sections.rule: 会 (huì) = a learned skill (我会说中文). 能 (néng) = physical ability or possibility in a situation (我今天能来). 可以 (kěyǐ) = permission (你可以走了).
sections.example_target: 我会说中文，但今天很累，不能说太多。
sections.example_ref: English: I can speak Chinese, but I'm tired today and can't speak much. / You may use my computer.
sections.note: pinyin: wǒ huì shuō Zhōngwén... 会 = knowing how; 能 = being able in the moment; 可以 = being allowed.

sections.title: 想 / 要 / 得 (Desire & Duty)
sections.rule: 想 (xiǎng) = want to / would like (softer wish): 我想喝茶. 要 (yào) = want / will / intend (firmer): 我要走了. 得 (děi) = have to / must: 你得去.
sections.example_target: 我想喝茶，但我得先工作。
sections.example_ref: English: I'd like to drink tea, but I have to work first. / I'm leaving now.
sections.note: pinyin: wǒ xiǎng hē chá, dàn wǒ děi xiān gōngzuò. 得 meaning 'must' is read děi, not de — its negative is 不用 (needn't), not 不得.

sections.title: The 被 Passive
sections.rule: Form the passive with Subject + 被 + (Agent) + Verb + extra element: 我的手机被偷了. The agent after 被 is optional. Often carries an unfortunate or unexpected tone.
sections.example_ref: English: My phone was stolen. / He was criticized by the teacher.
sections.note: pinyin: wǒ de shǒujī bèi tōu le. The verb needs an extra element (了, a complement) — bare 被 + verb sounds incomplete.

sections.title: 给 (gěi): Give / For / To
sections.rule: 给 can be a main verb 'to give' or a preposition marking the recipient/beneficiary: Subject + 给 + Person + Verb Phrase. 我给你打电话 (I'll call you), 请给我一杯水 (please give me a glass of water).
sections.example_ref: English: I'll call you. / Please give me a glass of water.
sections.note: pinyin: wǒ gěi nǐ dǎ diànhuà. As a preposition 给 + person comes before the verb; as 'give' it takes two objects after it.

sections.title: 因为...所以 / 虽然...但是
sections.rule: Chinese often keeps BOTH halves of a paired conjunction. 因为...所以 = because...so; 虽然...但是 = although...but. Both clauses stay linked even though English drops one word.
sections.example_ref: English: Because it's raining, I won't go. / Although it's expensive, it's good.
sections.note: pinyin: yīnwèi xià yǔ, suǒyǐ wǒ bú qù. Keeping both 因为...所以 is natural in Chinese, unlike English where you use only one.

sections.title: Imminent Action 要...了
sections.rule: 要...了 or 快...了 (also 快要...了) means 'about to happen soon': 火车要开了, 快下雨了. The 了 signals the imminent change of state.
sections.example_ref: English: The train is about to leave. / I'm almost there.
sections.note: pinyin: huǒchē yào kāi le. Add a time word for a specific deadline: 我们六点要走了 (we're about to leave at six).

sections.title: Verb Reduplication
sections.rule: Repeating a verb softens it into a brief, casual, or tentative action: 看看 (take a look), 试试 (give it a try), 休息休息 (rest a bit). One-syllable verbs may add 一: 想一想.
sections.example_ref: English: Take a look at this. / Let's rest a bit.
sections.note: pinyin: nǐ kànkan zhège. The second syllable is neutral tone (kànkan). It makes requests gentler and less demanding.

sections.title: 越来越 and 越...越
sections.rule: 越来越 + adjective = 'more and more' over time: 天气越来越冷. 越...越... links two changing factors: 越多越好 (the more the better), 越快越好 (the faster the better).
sections.example_ref: English: The weather is getting colder and colder. / The more things, the better.
sections.note: pinyin: tiānqì yuè lái yuè lěng. 越来越 needs a single adjective; 越...越 needs a verb/adjective on each 越.
